title: Browser Messaging and Workers
description: XHR, WebSocket, Web Worker, and Service Worker communication models and lifecycles.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish HTTP request/response, WebSocket, and worker use cases.
Handle XHR HTTP status separately from transport errors.
Manage WebSocket open/message/close, validation, cleanup, and reconnect policy.
Move computation to a Web Worker and assess structured-clone cost.
Explain Service Worker scope/lifecycle and limit caching safely.

blocks.text: Choose an API for its communication model. Fetch/XHR make an HTTP request and receive a response; WebSocket keeps a bidirectional message channel; a Web Worker moves computation off the main thread but has no DOM; a Service Worker intercepts eligible origin requests and manages cache/offline behavior. These solve different problems and have different lifecycles.

items: For new request/response work, prefer Fetch + AbortController; XHR remains useful for legacy code and specific upload/download progress events.
For repeated low-latency server messages, use WebSocket when the server supports it; the channel does not replace ordinary HTTP APIs.
For heavy synchronous CPU work, consider a Web Worker; it does not automatically make networking faster and cannot change the DOM.
A Service Worker lives separately from a tab and manages event-driven request/cache strategies, not UI components.

blocks.text: XHR: a legacy API with explicit HTTP status and failures

steps.title: Configure before sending
steps.explanation: Create XHR, call open, then set responseType/timeout before send. A GET has no body; POST requests set a method and headers.

steps.title: Separate HTTP failure from network failure
steps.explanation: load fires for HTTP 404/500 too; inspect status. error indicates a network-level failure, while timeout indicates the configured time limit elapsed.

steps.title: Handle completion
steps.explanation: Attach listeners before send so a quick event is not missed. Keep the request if UI needs to call abort() on cancellation/navigation.

steps.title: Send the request
steps.explanation: send runs after listeners are attached. To cancel, retain request and call abort from explicit cancellation/cleanup.

blocks.prompt: XHR fires load and status is 404. What does that mean?

options.text: The network necessarily failed before a response arrived.
options.feedback: A network failure is generally reported as error; 404 is an HTTP response.

options.text: The request completed with HTTP 404; the app must inspect status.
options.feedback: Correct. load by itself does not mean the HTTP status was successful.
If a status was received and load fired, the request was sent and completed with a response.

options.text: A timer will automatically retry the request.
options.feedback: XHR does not retry automatically; retry policy belongs to the application.

blocks.explanation: Transport outcome and HTTP status are separate layers. Inspect status in load and handle error/timeout/abort separately.

steps.title: Open a secure channel
steps.explanation: For an HTTPS app, generally use wss:. The connection passes through states; send only after open.

steps.title: Send and validate messages
steps.explanation: Check OPEN before send and define a message protocol. The server may send unexpected data; do not assume every message is JSON.

steps.title: Keep parse and transport errors distinct
steps.explanation: message data can be a string, Blob, or ArrayBuffer. try/catch handles malformed JSON; close/error are separate events.

steps.title: Close the lifecycle loop
steps.explanation: close includes a code/reason, while error signals a channel issue. Reconcile both with retry policy and do not reconnect after dispose.

blocks.title: WebSocket does not provide application backpressure
blocks.text: A high message rate can accumulate work and memory; monitor bufferedAmount and define a cap, coalescing, or drop policy. On reconnect, use bounded exponential backoff with jitter, stop after dispose, and resubscribe; do not blindly replay non-idempotent commands.

WebSocket does not reconnect by itself. Keep the connection reference, close it when its owner goes away (for example, in a React effect cleanup), distinguish intentional close from transient failure, and define recovery semantics. Close/retry must account for idempotency and resubscription.
Web Worker: heavy computation away from the UI thread

steps.title: Create a worker and send cloneable data
steps.explanation: In the main module, create a worker with a URL and send data rather than DOM references.

steps.title: Compute in the worker scope
steps.explanation: The main thread receives result/error and sends the request. A one-shot worker terminates after responding; repeated work needs explicit disposal.

steps.title: Render and release the worker
steps.explanation: The worker scope uses self rather than window/document and returns the result through a message.

blocks.prompt: What limits a dedicated Web Worker?

options.text: It cannot access the document DOM/window.
options.feedback: Correct. A worker has its own global scope and communicates through messages.
A worker runs JavaScript separately from the main UI thread.

options.text: It can only style DOM elements.
options.feedback: It has no DOM; computation and messaging are common uses.

options.text: It always blocks the main thread synchronously.
options.feedback: The purpose is to move work off the main thread; sending large data still has a cost.

blocks.explanation: A dedicated Web Worker cannot access window/document DOM. Communication with the document uses postMessage and structured data.

blocks.text: A worker helps with CPU-bound work when the time saved is worth serialization/copy overhead. structured clone copies supported values; Transferables such as ArrayBuffer can move ownership, detaching the sender's buffer. Tiny tasks or huge payloads may be slower in a worker.
Service Worker: install, activate, and fetch

steps.title: Register the service worker
steps.explanation: Registration attaches the worker to a scope. Production usually needs a secure context; localhost is allowed for development.

steps.title: Prepare cache during install
steps.explanation: event.waitUntil keeps the event alive until the operation settles. Cache explicitly chosen static assets and version the cache deliberately.

steps.title: Intercept only eligible requests
steps.explanation: A fetch handler must call respondWith for an intercepted request. This cache-first example is limited to same-origin GET; do not apply it blindly to personal/API responses. The cache-first response is limited to same-origin GET; do not apply it to personal/API responses without a privacy policy.

items: A dedicated Web Worker belongs to an application/document, computes and exchanges messages, and can be terminated by the app; it has no DOM.
A Service Worker is not tied to one open tab, starts for events, has a scope and can mediate network/cache requests; its lifecycle and updates need versioning.
Both use separate global scopes; do not confuse self with window or send DOM nodes through messages.
XHR is mostly for legacy/progress needs; prefer Fetch with explicit cancellation and HTTP-status handling for new request/response work.

blocks.title: Move sorting off the main thread
blocks.context: A page sorts a large set of numbers and starts dropping frames. Design a module worker that sorts a copy, returns a typed result, and is cleaned up when the page leaves.
instructions: Implement createSorter(onResult, onError), creating a Worker with new URL(..., import.meta.url) and type: module.
Define a request/response message with type and payload; ignore invalid type/data.
In the worker, sort a copied numeric array without mutating the input, then post a result.
Deliver the result through a main-thread callback, handle message/error, and return dispose() that calls terminate().
Explain structured-clone cost and when an ArrayBuffer transfer list is useful; do not promise a speedup for tiny arrays.
requirements: Worker code does not access document/window DOM.
Both incoming and outgoing messages are validated by type/shape.
Sorting copies before mutation and returns deterministic order.
UI callback runs only for a valid result; worker errors reach the handler.
dispose stops the worker and leaves no application listeners behind.
Trade-off between CPU benefit, worker startup, and data copy is explained.
hints: Define a small protocol such as { type: 'sort', values } and { type: 'sorted', values }; validate both boundaries.
Use [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b) to avoid mutating the received logical input.
Only the main thread should update DOM or component state.
Call terminate from dispose; if the worker is reusable, decide whether to keep it alive or terminate after one result.
successCriteria: Sorting runs in the worker and output is deterministic numeric order.
Invalid message shapes do not crash the page or invoke onResult.
Error events reach onError and dispose stops the worker.
Explanation weighs CPU benefit against startup and structured-clone cost.

items: XHR is an event-driven legacy HTTP API; inspect HTTP status separately from network/timeout/abort events.
WebSocket is a persistent full-duplex channel with explicit lifecycle, message validation, cleanup, and app-owned retry/backpressure policy.
Dedicated workers move CPU work off the UI thread but have no DOM; structured clone/transfer has cost.
Service workers are event-driven, origin-scoped proxies for network/cache and offline strategies, not background UI threads.
Use secure contexts, same-origin/scope rules, conservative caching, and lifecycle cleanup deliberately.
